client: I've been really struggling lately with this huge group project I got assigned at university. There's going to be a final presentation in front of the whole class, and just thinking about it makes my chest tighten and my mind go blank. I'm not even sure talking about it here is going to change anything, because the presentation is still going to happen no matter what.
therapist: It sounds like this presentation is weighing on you in a very real, physical way — that chest tightening and mind going blank are your body's way of signaling how much this matters to you. You're right that the presentation will still happen, and I think that's actually a useful starting point — since we can't change that fact, we can focus on what *is* within your control, like how you relate to the thoughts that are making it feel so overwhelming. What is it specifically about the presentation that your mind keeps coming back to most — is it the judgment of others, going blank in the moment, something else?

client: I think it's mostly the judgment from others, honestly. Like, I keep imagining everyone in the class watching me stumble over my words or forget what I was supposed to say, and then just thinking I'm incompetent. And the worst part is some of these people are in my program, so it's not like I can just never see them again — I have to keep running into them after.
therapist: That fear of being permanently judged by people you can't avoid makes a lot of sense — it adds a layer of stakes that makes the whole thing feel much heavier than a one-time event. I'd gently invite you to examine that core thought though: if you *did* stumble over some words, what's the evidence that your classmates would actually conclude you're incompetent, rather than just... human? What do you notice when you watch *other* people struggle a little during presentations — do you tend to write them off, or do you usually see them differently than you fear others see you?

client: Okay, I can see what you're getting at — when other people stumble in presentations, I don't usually think they're incompetent, I mostly just feel kind of bad for them and move on. But it feels different when it's me, like the rules are somehow different and people will remember it more or judge me harder. I know that probably sounds irrational when I say it out loud, but the feeling is still really strong even when I try to logic my way out of it.
therapist: You've just done something really important — you caught the double standard your mind is applying to yourself versus others, and naming it out loud like that takes real self-awareness. That gap between *knowing* something intellectually and *feeling* it differently is incredibly common, and it doesn't mean you're failing at thinking clearly — it just means this belief has been around long enough to feel like truth. What do you think that belief — that the rules are different for you — might be protecting you from, or where do you think it first came from?

client: That's a hard question to sit with. I think maybe it goes back to a time in high school where I gave a presentation and completely froze, and people were visibly uncomfortable watching me, and a few of them brought it up afterward in a way that felt humiliating. So maybe the belief isn't totally irrational — it actually happened once, and I guess part of me is convinced it's just who I am when I'm in front of people.
therapist: That experience sounds genuinely painful, and it makes complete sense that your mind held onto it so tightly — being humiliated in front of peers at that age leaves a real mark. But I want to gently challenge one piece: one very hard moment in high school became a story about *who you are*, when it might be more accurate to see it as something that *happened to you* once, under pressure, years ago. What evidence do you have from your life since then — even small moments — that might not fit the identity of "someone who always freezes in front of people"?

client: I mean, I guess there have been a few times — like last semester I had to explain my research idea to a smaller seminar group and it actually went okay, people asked questions and seemed genuinely interested. But I keep dismissing those moments as "not counting" because the stakes felt lower or the group was smaller. I'm not sure how to make those memories feel as real and relevant as the bad one, because the high school memory just hits so much harder emotionally.
therapist: You've just caught another really important pattern — your mind has a filtering system that automatically disqualifies the good evidence while keeping the painful memory on a pedestal, and that's actually a very common cognitive habit called *discounting the positive*. The seminar moment is just as real as the high school one — people asked questions, they were engaged, that happened — and the fact that it feels less vivid doesn't make it less true. What do you think it would mean for your sense of yourself if you *did* allow that seminar moment to count as genuine evidence of who you are in front of others?

client: I think if I actually let that seminar moment count, it would mean I'm not just "the person who freezes" — and honestly that's kind of uncomfortable to sit with, because that identity has been with me for so long that it almost feels safer to hold onto it than to risk believing something different and then being proven wrong again. Like, if I let myself think I can do this and then I freeze at the presentation anyway, that would feel so much worse than just expecting the worst from the start. So I guess I'm protecting myself by keeping the bar low, even though I can see it's also keeping me stuck.
therapist: What you just described is a really profound insight — that the old identity, as painful as it is, feels like a shield against future disappointment, and there's something almost logical about that protection even as you can see the cost it carries. That tension between "staying safe by expecting the worst" and "risking hope" is one of the most human struggles there is, and the fact that you can name it so clearly suggests you're already loosening its grip a little. I'm curious — if a close friend described this exact reasoning to you, that they were keeping themselves stuck to avoid being hurt, what would you want them to know?

client: I'd probably tell a friend that one bad experience doesn't define them, and that they deserve to give themselves a real chance instead of just bracing for the worst all the time. But when I try to turn that around on myself, it feels almost hollow, like I'm just saying the right words without really believing them. I think part of me is worried that being compassionate toward myself about this is somehow naive, like I'd just be setting myself up for a harder fall.
therapist: That gap between the wisdom you'd offer a friend and being able to truly receive it yourself is something so many people struggle with — self-compassion can feel dangerously naive when you've learned that hoping hurts. But I want to reflect something back: believing in yourself isn't the same as guaranteeing a perfect outcome, it just means you deserve the same fair chance you'd give anyone else, regardless of how it goes. What do you think it would actually look like, in small and concrete terms, to give yourself that real chance in the lead-up to this presentation — not to promise it'll go perfectly, but just to stop automatically bracing for the worst?

client: I think concretely it might look like actually practicing out loud instead of just running through it in my head, because when I do it in my head I can control everything and avoid the discomfort. But I'm already feeling resistant to that idea because practicing out loud, even alone, means actually confronting the possibility of stumbling, and I'm not sure I can handle that without it just reinforcing my fears. I guess I'm worried that practicing will just become another way for me to collect evidence against myself rather than for myself.
therapist: You've already identified something really wise — that the safety of rehearsing in your head is actually a way of avoiding the very experience you need to build real confidence, and that takes honesty to admit. The fear that practice will just become evidence *against* you makes sense, but it's worth considering that stumbling during a low-stakes solo practice and *continuing anyway* is actually the opposite of the high school experience — it would be proof that you can recover, not proof that you can't. What if the goal of practicing out loud wasn't to be perfect, but specifically to practice what it feels like to stumble and keep going — would that change how the idea feels?

client: That reframe actually does shift something slightly — like, if the point isn't to perform perfectly but to practice surviving the stumble, that feels a little less like setting myself up for failure. But I'm still not sure I trust myself to interpret it that way in the moment, because I know once I start stumbling I'll probably just spiral into "see, this is exactly what happens" rather than "I'm practicing recovery." I think I'd need some kind of anchor to hold onto in the moment to stop myself from going down that path — I just don't know what that would look like yet.
therapist: It's really encouraging that the reframe shifted something for you, even slightly — that matters. An anchor is a great instinct, and in CBT we often call this a "coping statement" — a short, specific phrase you decide on *before* the spiral starts, so it's ready when your mind tries to pull you into "see, this is what always happens." Something like *"stumbling is the practice, not the proof"* could work, but the most powerful anchor is usually one that comes from your own words — so I'm curious, based on everything you've uncovered today, what's one true thing about yourself that you think you could actually hold onto in that moment?

client: Maybe something like "I've done this before and people actually engaged" — because that seminar moment is real, even if it doesn't feel as loud as the bad memory. I think I could try to hold onto that, but I'm a little worried that in the heat of the moment, when my chest is tight and my mind is going blank, that sentence is just going to feel like a lie I'm telling myself rather than something I actually believe. I guess the honest question is whether any of this work we've done today will actually be accessible to me when I'm standing up there in front of everyone.
therapist: The anchor you chose is perfect precisely because it's grounded in something that actually happened — "I've done this before and people engaged" isn't a motivational phrase, it's a fact, and that's what gives it real weight. Your worry about accessing all of this under pressure is completely valid, and it points to something important: the work we do in reflection doesn't automatically transfer to high-stress moments, which is exactly why practicing out loud — including saying that anchor out loud when you stumble — is how you build that bridge between knowing it and feeling it. What might it look like to build even one small moment this week where you practice both the stumble *and* the anchor together, so your mind and body start to learn that the recovery is part of the process?
